To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

N- and P- based dairy manure applications did supply similar amounts of N for crop growth, but that the N-based manures led to significantly higher soil test P in surface soil, which may lead to greater P losses off the field in the future.
N-based and P-based manures were equally effective at supplying nutrients for crop growth and reducing N leaching losses, but the N-based treatment increased accumulation of soil P.
N- and P- based applications of dairy manure were similar in ability to supply N and P to crops, but the N-based manures caused a greater accumulation of P in the surface soil.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of N vs. P-based dairy manure management practices for field crops on nitrate and
the effects of manure application on nitrate and phosphorous leaching and soil P accumulation.

N- or P-based manure application to a crop does not affect the amount of nitrate or total P leached from the soil profile, but N-based manure application does lead to accumulation of soil test phosphorus.
N- and P- based manure application rates can be applied at the same rate, without any significant differences in nitrate or phosphorus losses.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
N-based manure applications are not recommended for crops that are not P limited, and that N-based manures should be avoided in situations where surface soil P accumulation is undesirable.
manure management based on crop N requirements is not necessarily the best management for the environment.

The main takeaway from our work is that
P management should receive greater attention in manure management programs, and should be based on crop P requirements, rather than crop N requirements.
